differentiation.support: Provide the student notes open at the hydrogen ion and hydroxide ion definitions so learners can follow which ion is in excess before judging the pH.

activities.title: What pH is really about: ions

differentiation.stretch: Ask learners to explain why vinegar is still an acid even though it only partly releases its hydrogen ions before they take the exit ticket.

activities.title: A common mistake: all acids are strong
The titration curve: watch for the jump

assessmentPoints: Everyday-substance answers in the opening activity
Ladder answers in the second activity and the closing worksheet
successCriteria: I can classify lemon juice and vinegar as acids and soap and baking soda as alkalis
I can read the pH scale from 0 to 14, place 7 as neutral, and say each step is ten times stronger
objectives.text: Read the pH scale and classify a solution as acidic, neutral or alkaline

assessmentPoints: Ion answers in the third activity
Neutralisation answers in the fourth activity and the closing worksheet
successCriteria: I can state that acids release H+ ions and alkalis release OH- ions in water
I can explain that whichever ion is in excess decides whether a solution is acidic or alkaline
objectives.text: Explain acidity and alkalinity in terms of H+ and OH- ions

assessmentPoints: Salt-naming answers in the sixth activity
Titration answers in the eighth activity and the closing exit ticket
successCriteria: I can write acid plus alkali gives salt plus water and name a chloride, nitrate or sulfate from its acid
I can point to the vertical jump on a titration curve and call it the equivalence point
objectives.text: Describe neutralisation, name salts from their acids, and read the jump on a titration curve
